about: Risk profile R4 (docs/risk-profile/01-plan.md): the home and water checklist. No validated instrument scores these, so each is an exposure present or not, with its source and its fix; there is no score. An item is flagged when its answer is in 'flag'. Answered once, asked again after 12 months.

items.question: How do you cook at home?
options: Gas, with the hood on or a window open
items.why: Gas burners give off nitrogen dioxide and fine particles; without extraction they build up indoors.
items.fix: Run the hood on its highest setting or open a window while cooking and for 10 minutes after; induction removes the source.
items.source: WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: selected pollutants (2010), nitrogen dioxide; WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel combustion (2014).

items.question: Do you burn incense or candles indoors?
items.why: Burning incense and candles is an indoor source of fine particles and other combustion products.
items.fix: Burn less often, ventilate while burning, or use a HEPA purifier in that room.
items.source: WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: household fuel combustion (2014), indoor combustion sources.

items.question: Do you heat food or drinks in plastic containers (microwave, hot drinks in plastic cups)?
items.why: Heat increases the migration of plastic additives (such as bisphenols and phthalates) into food.
items.fix: Heat food in glass or ceramic; let hot food cool before it goes into plastic.
items.source: EFSA re-evaluation of bisphenol A (2023); US FDA guidance on microwaving food in plastic.

items.question: Do you heat non-stick pans empty or on the highest heat?
items.why: PTFE (non-stick) coatings start to break down at high temperatures (above about 260 °C), giving off fumes; an empty pan on high heat can get there in minutes.
items.fix: Do not preheat non-stick pans empty or on high; use stainless steel or cast iron for searing.
items.source: Reports of polymer fume fever from overheated PTFE; manufacturers' and food-safety agency guidance on maximum temperatures.

items.question: Is there visible mould or a damp, musty smell anywhere in your home?
items.why: Dampness and mould go with more respiratory symptoms, asthma and respiratory infections.
items.fix: Fix the source of moisture, ventilate the bathroom and kitchen, keep indoor humidity under about 60 % (the home sensors show it), clean small patches.
items.source: WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: dampness and mould (2009).

items.question: Has your home been tested for radon?
options: No, but I live above the second floor
items.why: Radon is the second cause of lung cancer after smoking; homes on or below ground are where it collects.
items.fix: Above 100 Bq/m³: improve under-floor ventilation or sealing (a radon specialist can advise). Untested and on the ground floor: a long-term test kit is inexpensive.
items.source: WHO handbook on indoor radon (2009): reference level 100 Bq/m³.

items.question: What do you drink at home?
options: Private well, not tested in the last year
Private well, tested in the last year
items.why: Mains water is tested by the supplier; a private well is not, and can carry nitrate, arsenic or microbes.
items.fix: Test a private well at least once a year (microbes, nitrate) and after floods; treat as the result requires.
items.source: WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality (4th ed., 2022 addenda).
